title: About those ‘genius kid’ stories
author: Educating Hatbeasts
summary: Writing as a home educator of an academically precocious son, the author takes apart the recurring news template of the genius child who joins Mensa or starts college at thirteen. The first myths she tackles are statistical: Mensa's cutoff of 132 is the top 2%, roughly seven children in every American elementary school, and IQ scores reported at 168 or 195 exceed what tests like the WISC can reliably measure, often because reporters use obsolete ratio IQs. She then turns more serious, arguing that gifted children working far above grade level represent a genuine special educational need that many teachers dismiss, and that acceleration has strong research support but is hard to arrange. The danger, she argues, lies at the extreme, where children cognitively ready for university are emotionally and socially unready for it, as the cases of Cameron Thompson and Laurent Simons illustrate. She ends with a set of questions parents and journalists should ask, especially about who is driving the push toward qualifications and publicity.
points: A Mensa-level IQ of 132 describes about one child in fifty, so most so-called geniuses in news stories are simply bright children whose parents sought a test.
The WISC tops out at 160 and is considered unreliable above about 145, making headline IQs of 168 or 195 largely meaningless.
She argues that if children two or three standard deviations below average need a modified education, so do those equally far above it.
Acceleration has long-term research support, but at the far end of giftedness schools cannot flex enough to accommodate a child meaningfully.
Her closing checklist asks whether the child or the parents are driving early college and whether the child is socially ready for it.
quotes: MENSA’s IQ test requires a full-scale IQ of 132, the top 2% of the population, which sounds impressive but is, statistically speaking, one in every 50 children.

Thus, when someone quotes an IQ score of 168 or even 195 on a WISC, all you really know is that they’re likely smarter than 99.9% of kids, which makes them at least 1 in 1,000 for the rarity of their learning profile.
Putting the silly IQ stuff aside, a child working significantly above grade level poses an educational challenge. It’s a type of special educational need.
If you reflect on that, 145 is as far above an average IQ as someone near the bottom of their class at a special school is below.

The difficulty is, although acceleration within school can work brilliantly for kids who are one or two years ahead, at some level of giftedness, schools simply can’t flex enough for a child to meaningfully remain there.
If you’re someone who is cognitively 19 before your 10th birthday, this causes huge social and structural problems for your education.
Who is pushing the focus on formal qualifications and college courses - the child or the parents?
